syllabus_version.title: CBSE Curriculum for the Academic Year 2026-27

concepts.learning_objective: Describe science as a way of thinking, observing and doing things to understand the world, driven by curiosity.
Recognise that science is found everywhere, from the kitchen and playground to the ocean and outer space.
Explain why science is compared to an unending jigsaw puzzle whose pieces can change with new discoveries.

topics.title: What will we explore with the help of this book?

concepts.learning_objective: Identify Earth as the only known planet that supports life and the questions about how plants and animals grow.
Frame scientific questions about food, materials, water and hot and cold from everyday experience.

topics.title: How can we find answers to our questions on our own?

concepts.learning_objective: State and order the steps of the scientific method: observe, question, guess, test and analyse.
Apply the idea of testing a guess and making a new guess when the first one is not supported.

topics.title: We are all, in a way, scientists

concepts.learning_objective: Recognise the scientific method in daily-life situations such as cooking, repairing a tyre or fixing a bulb.
Explain that science is rarely done alone and that scientists often work together in teams.
Explain why being curious and asking 'how' and 'why' is the first step to learning science.

topics.title: Diversity in Plants and Animals Around Us

concepts.learning_objective: Observe and record the features of plants and animals around us without disturbing them.
Explain biodiversity as the variety of living things in a region and how plants and animals depend on each other.
Explain why grouping living things by similarities and differences makes them easier to study.
Identify and apply a common feature as the basis for grouping plants and animals.

topics.title: Herbs, Shrubs, Trees, Climbers and Creepers

concepts.learning_objective: Classify plants as herbs, shrubs or trees by height, nature of stem and branching.
Distinguish climbers and creepers as plants with weak stems.
Distinguish reticulate and parallel venation in leaves.
Distinguish taproots and fibrous roots and relate them to leaf venation.
Group plants as monocots or dicots by the number of cotyledons and relate this to roots and venation.
Identify the types of movement in animals and the body parts they use.

topics.title: Plants and Animals in Different Surroundings: Adaptations

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how features of desert and mountain plants help them survive their surroundings.
Explain how the features of camels in hot and cold deserts help them survive.
Define habitat and group living things as terrestrial, aquatic or amphibians.
Explain how habitat damage causes loss of biodiversity and how it can be protected.

chapters.title: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body

topics.title: Food diversity across regions of India

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why the food eaten by people varies across the regions of India.
Relate the traditional food of a state to the crops grown locally.
Distinguish traditional cooking and grinding tools from their modern replacements.
Identify the factors that have changed cooking practices over time.
Identify carbohydrates and their sources as primary energy-giving foods.
Recognise fats and their plant and animal sources as stored energy.
Explain why proteins are called body-building foods and name their sources.
Match vitamins and minerals with their functions, sources and deficiency diseases.
Explain the roles of dietary fibres and water in the body.
Explain how cooking and washing cut vegetables can cause loss of some vitamins.

topics.title: Testing food for starch, fats and proteins

concepts.learning_objective: Describe and interpret the iodine test for starch.
Describe and interpret the oily-patch paper test for fats.
Describe and interpret the copper sulfate and caustic soda test for proteins.
Define a balanced diet and explain why nutritional needs vary between people.
Use nutritional information to identify junk food and explain why it is unhealthy.
Explain why millets are called nutri-cereals and how they support a balanced diet.
Explain what fortified foods are, with examples.

topics.title: Food miles: from farm to our plate

concepts.learning_objective: Define food miles and explain the benefits of reducing them.
Sequence the steps by which food such as wheat reaches our plate.
Explain why we should avoid wasting food.
Distinguish naturally occurring magnets (lodestones) from the artificial magnets used in everyday objects.
Classify materials as magnetic or non-magnetic and name iron, nickel and cobalt as magnetic metals.
Identify the poles as the parts of a magnet where its attraction is strongest.
Explain that North and South poles always occur in pairs, whatever the size or shape of the magnet.
Explain that a freely suspended magnet rests along the north-south direction and use this to tell a magnet from an iron bar.
Describe the parts of a magnetic compass and how it is used to find directions.

topics.title: Making a magnet and a compass

concepts.learning_objective: Describe how an iron needle is made into a magnet by stroking it with one pole of a magnet and how to test it.
Explain how a magnetised needle on a floating cork, or the matsya-yantra, works as a compass.
State that unlike poles attract and like poles repel, and apply this to magnets and compass needles.
Use repulsion to tell a magnet from a piece of iron.
Recognise that the magnetic effect acts through non-magnetic materials such as wood, cardboard, plastic and glass.

topics.title: Fun with magnets and caring for magnets

concepts.learning_objective: Apply the properties of magnets to solve everyday problems and explain magnet-based toys.
State how magnets should be stored and handled so that they stay strong.
Explain why lengths measured with body parts such as the handspan or stride differ from person to person.
State that a measured length is expressed in two parts, a number and a unit.
Identify the metre as the SI unit of length and distinguish standard from non-standard units.
Convert lengths between kilometre, metre, centimetre and millimetre.
Choose a suitable scale or tape for measuring a given length.
Describe the correct placement of a scale and the correct position of the eye while reading it.
Measure a length with a scale whose ends are broken by subtracting the starting mark reading.

topics.title: Measuring the Length of a Curved Line

concepts.learning_objective: Measure the length of a curved line using a thread or flexible tape and apply it to find distances.
Write lengths with the correct unit symbols, spacing and lowercase letters.
Define a reference point and identify it in everyday situations.
Interpret how the position of an object changes with respect to a reference point.
Decide whether an object is at rest or in motion from the change in its position with time.
Explain that the same object can be at rest or in motion depending on the chosen reference point.

topics.title: Types of Motion: Linear and Circular Motion

concepts.learning_objective: Identify linear motion as motion along a straight line.
Identify circular motion as motion along a circular path.

topics.title: Types of Motion: Oscillatory and Periodic Motion

concepts.learning_objective: Identify oscillatory motion as to-and-fro motion about a fixed position.
Explain that circular and oscillatory motions are periodic because the path repeats after a fixed interval of time.
Define a material as any substance used to create an object.
Recognise that objects are made of one or more materials and that one material can make many objects.
Explain classification as arranging objects or materials into groups on the basis of a common property.
Explain that a material is chosen for an object according to its properties and the purpose of the object.
Distinguish lustrous from non-lustrous materials and explain why some metals look dull.
Classify materials as hard or soft and recognise that hardness is a relative property.
Classify materials as transparent, translucent or opaque by how clearly objects can be seen through them.
Relate the transparency of a material to its everyday use.
Classify solids as soluble or insoluble in water from observations of mixing.
Recognise that some liquids and gases mix or dissolve in water while others do not.
Describe mass as the property that tells how heavy or light an object is.
Describe volume as the space occupied by a substance.
Define matter as anything that has mass and occupies space.
Use and correctly write the units of mass and volume, including simple conversions.
Explain why our sense of touch cannot always correctly judge whether a body is hot or cold.
Predict how the same water feels to hands that were earlier kept in warm and in cold water.
State that temperature is a reliable measure of the hotness or coldness of a body and compare bodies by it.
Identify a thermometer as the device for measuring temperature and distinguish clinical from laboratory thermometers by use.
Describe the digital clinical thermometer and why it has replaced the mercury thermometer.
List the steps and precautions for measuring body temperature with a digital clinical thermometer.
Interpret normal body temperature as an average and relate armpit readings to actual body temperature.
Name the Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin scales, their units and the SI unit of temperature.
Convert a temperature from the Celsius scale to the Kelvin scale.
Write temperatures and their unit symbols correctly.

topics.title: Laboratory thermometer: range and smallest value

concepts.learning_objective: Describe the parts of a laboratory thermometer and its usual range.
Calculate the smallest value a thermometer can read and use it to take a reading.

topics.title: Measuring temperature with a laboratory thermometer

concepts.learning_objective: Follow the correct way of measuring the temperature of water with a laboratory thermometer.
Recognise that water stays at a constant temperature while boiling and ice while melting.
Interpret maximum and minimum air temperatures from weather reports and their use in forecasts.
Recall Anna Mani's contribution to weather measurement instruments in India.

chapters.title: A Journey through States of Water

topics.title: Ice, Water and Water's Disappearing Act

concepts.learning_objective: Recognise that ice and water are two states of the same substance.
Define evaporation and identify everyday examples of water changing into water vapour.
Explain that water vapour is invisible and that steam is visible because of tiny water droplets.
Define condensation as the change of water vapour into liquid water on a cold surface.
Use observations from the tumbler activities to show that outside droplets come from condensation, not seepage.
Compare solid, liquid and gaseous states by shape, flow and spreading.
Classify common substances as solids, liquids or gases.
Define melting and freezing and give examples from daily life.
Explain that substances change state when they are heated or cooled.
Link melting, freezing, evaporation and condensation to the states they connect.

topics.title: Making Water Evaporate Faster or Slower

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how a larger exposed area makes water evaporate faster.
Describe how heat, air movement and humidity affect the rate of evaporation.
Identify the condition changed and the conditions kept the same in an evaporation investigation.
Explain that evaporation produces a cooling effect, with everyday examples.
Explain how an earthen pot and a pot-in-pot cooler keep things cool.

topics.title: Clouds, Rain and the Water Cycle

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how clouds and rain form through condensation of water vapour around dust particles.
Describe the water cycle as the circulation of water between the Earth's surface and the atmosphere.
Explain why only a small part of the Earth's water is usable and why water must be used wisely.

chapters.title: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life

concepts.learning_objective: Explain when and on what basis handpicking is used to separate a solid mixture.
Describe threshing as beating stalks to separate grains and place it in the sequence of grain processing.
Explain how wind or blown air separates heavier and lighter components of a mixture.
State that threshers carry out threshing and winnowing together.
Explain that sieving separates solids whose particles differ in size.
Relate the size of the holes of a sieve to which particles pass through and which remain.
Explain how evaporation separates a solid dissolved in a liquid.
Describe how common salt is obtained from seawater using sunlight and air.
Define sedimentation as the settling of a heavier insoluble component in a liquid.
Explain decantation and its everyday uses and limits.
Explain how filtration separates insoluble solids from a liquid and name the residue and filtrate.
Choose a suitable filter based on the size of its pores and of the particles to be removed.
Explain how churning separates butter from curd or cream from milk.
Use the magnetic nature of substances such as iron to separate them from a mixture.
Distinguish separating two useful components from removing an unwanted one.
Match a mixture to a suitable method of separation.
Plan a sequence of methods to separate a mixture of more than two components.

topics.title: What sets the living apart: movement, growth and respiration

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how living beings, including plants such as Drosera and climbers, show movement and why movement alone does not make a thing living.
State that living beings grow and need food (nutrition) for growth and development.
Describe breathing as part of respiration in animals and the role of stomata in plants.

topics.title: Excretion, response to stimuli, reproduction and death

concepts.learning_objective: Identify excretion as the removal of waste products in animals (sweat, urine) and in plants (droplets on leaves).
Define a stimulus and give examples of responses to stimuli in animals and plants such as touch-me-not and amla.
Explain why reproduction is needed for the continuity of life and when a living being is said to be dead.

topics.title: Essential conditions for germination of a seed

concepts.learning_objective: Interpret the four-pot experiment to identify the conditions needed for bean seeds to germinate.
Explain how water softens the seed coat and how air in soil spaces helps germination.
State that most seeds do not need light to germinate but seedlings need sunlight to grow further.
Predict that roots grow downwards and shoots grow upwards even when a seedling is inverted.
Explain that a shoot bends towards light coming from one direction while the root keeps growing downwards.
Recall that J. C. Bose built the crescograph to record plant growth and responses to stimuli.
Arrange the stages in the life cycle of a bean plant from seed to fruit and death.
Explain how seeds formed in the fruit start a new generation, making the process a cycle.
Sequence the egg, larva, pupa and adult stages of a mosquito and describe where each lives.
Explain how removing stagnant water or spraying kerosene disrupts the mosquito life cycle.
Sequence the spawn, embryo, tadpole, froglet and adult stages in the life cycle of a frog.
Relate the changes in body features and habitat during a frog's life cycle to how each stage survives.
Recall the composition of air and the share of each gas in it.
Explain why living beings need oxygen from air to survive.
Describe wind as moving air and how its energy is used in windmills.
Explain why only a small fraction of Earth's water is usable freshwater.
Suggest ways to reduce wastage and pollution of water.
Describe rainwater harvesting and traditional stepwells as ways to conserve water.
Explain that the Sun is the main source of energy for all living beings.
Identify uses of the Sun's heat and light, including solar devices.
Explain how forests provide food, shelter and enrich the soil.
Describe efforts such as Van Mahotsav and the Chipko movement to protect forests.
Describe how soil is formed and what it contains.
Identify common rocks and their uses, and why rocks must be conserved.
State that rocks are made of minerals from which useful metals are extracted.
Explain how fossil fuels are formed and why their supply is limited.
Identify fossil fuels and their uses in transport, cooking and electricity.
Suggest ways to reduce the use of fossil fuels and the air pollution they cause.
Distinguish natural resources from human-made resources.
Classify resources that are replenished within a reasonable period as renewable.
Classify resources that are limited and not replenished as non-renewable.
Suggest alternatives that reduce air pollution caused by fossil fuels.
Relate daily activities to natural resources and explain using them responsibly.
Explain what constellations are and why recognising star patterns was useful for finding directions.
Identify Orion, Canis Major, Taurus and the star Sirius, and use Orion's belt to locate Sirius.
Relate Indian names such as nakshatras, Ardra, Krittika and Rohini to stars and groups of stars.

topics.title: The Pole Star and night sky watching

concepts.learning_objective: Use the Big Dipper to locate the Pole Star and explain how the Pole Star shows the North direction.
Explain how light pollution, smoke, dust and obstacles reduce the number of stars we can see.
Plan a safe and effective night sky watching session.
Describe the Sun as a star and the main source of heat and light on Earth, and explain why other stars are not seen by day.
Interpret the size and distance of the Sun and use the astronomical unit to express distances.
Define a planet and revolution, and explain why Pluto is now called a dwarf planet.
State the order of the eight planets and describe features of the inner and outer planets.
Distinguish planets from stars in the night sky and locate Venus at dawn or dusk.
Describe natural satellites and features of the Moon, including its craters and India's Chandrayaan missions.
Describe asteroids and the location of the asteroid belt.
Explain how a comet's tail forms and why comets are seen only near the Sun.

topics.title: The Solar System, the Milky Way Galaxy and the Universe

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the members of the Solar System and explain why objects other than the Sun shine.
Describe the Milky Way Galaxy as our home galaxy of which the Solar System is a part.
Explain what exoplanets are and describe the ongoing search for life in the Universe.
